planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; this San Pedro-type fig sets a reliable breba crop on old wood, so avoid hard winter pruning if the main summer crop is desired.

directions: Grantham's Royal is a San Pedro-type fig, meaning it reliably produces a large breba (first) crop on the previous year's wood but needs fig wasp pollination for a true second main crop, which rarely occurs outside the Mediterranean's native range. The large, deep-purple fruit has jammy, richly flavored red flesh with berry and peach notes that collectors rank among the best-tasting of all fig varieties. It is hardy to roughly 0-5°F, tolerating cooler summers better than many Mediterranean fig cultivars, making it a favorite among Pacific Northwest and coastal California growers.

common_name: Col de Dame Noir Fig (Coll de Dama Negra)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, fertile soil against a warm south-facing wall; this late-ripening dark fig needs a long, hot season to fully sweeten before frost.

directions: Col de Dame Noir is a black-skinned counterpart to the more widely known Col de Dame Blanc, sharing the same elongated, narrow-necked fruit shape said to resemble an old French collar or necklace. The dense, deep-red flesh inside near-black skin is exceptionally sweet and rich, prized by fig collectors for drying as well as fresh eating. As a late-season fig it demands a long, warm growing season, ripening well into fall in climates with mild autumns.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in full sun on well-drained soil; Wellington is self-fertile and needs no pollinator, and its cold hardiness makes it a reliable choice where true black mulberries are otherwise marginal.

directions: Wellington is a historic black mulberry selection traced to a tree on the New York property of pomologist Richard Wellington and long grown through the New York State Fruit Testing Cooperative at Geneva, valued as one of the hardiest true black-fruited mulberries available for northern gardens. The medium, cylindrical fruit ripens over several weeks in mid-to-late summer, extending the harvest window, with a rich, sweet-tart flavor well suited to fresh eating and preserves. Trees tolerate temperatures well below 0°F and adapt to a range of soils as long as drainage is adequate.
sources: Cornell University College of Agriculture and Life Sciences

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in full to partial sun on well-drained soil; Oscar is self-fertile, vigorous, and benefits from annual pruning to keep it at a manageable home-orchard size.

directions: Oscar is a red-white mulberry hybrid named for naturalist Oscar Clark, prized for early-ripening fruit that can be picked at the red stage for a tart, raspberry-like flavor or left to fully darken for a rich, blackberry-like taste. It is a fast-growing, easy-care tree that responds well to pruning and training, making it practical to keep at a manageable home-orchard height despite naturally vigorous growth. Ripening runs through mid-to-late summer, and the tree tolerates cold well into USDA zone 5.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container plants in early spring in cool, well-drained soil; Tixia's reduced, softer thorns make harvest noticeably easier than older English-type cultivars.

directions: Tixia is a Swiss-bred gooseberry raised from a cross with Invicta as the female parent, selected for large, bright red, sweet-tart berries on a vigorous, upright, mildew-resistant bush. A distinguishing trait is fewer thorns on first-year wood, and the thorns that remain stay soft, making picking substantially more comfortable than on traditional gooseberry cultivars. It performs best in regions with cool summers and consistent moisture, and struggles in prolonged heat or drought.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container plants in early spring in fertile, well-drained soil; Jeanne is self-fertile and its strong powdery mildew resistance makes it a low-maintenance choice for home plantings.

directions: Jeanne is a modern American-European hybrid gooseberry released by the USDA Agricultural Research Service, bred for high resistance to powdery mildew and other fungal diseases that commonly trouble older gooseberry cultivars. It produces medium-sized, deep maroon-red fruit with a full, sweet flavor considered an improvement over many traditional cultivars, ripening later in the season than most. The compact 2-3 foot bush bears reliably without a pollinator and is especially well suited to the Pacific Northwest and other cool, temperate climates.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container plants in early spring in fertile, well-drained soil; pair with Jogranda for best cross-pollination, and its thornless canes make maintenance easier than gooseberry parents.

directions: Jostine is a thornless, disease-resistant jostaberry cultivar prized for its compact growth habit, making it well suited to small gardens or container culture. It produces medium-to-large, deep violet berries with a complex, tart-forward flavor that ripens slightly later than the original Josta cultivar, extending the harvest into midsummer. Fruit holds well on the bush after ripening, giving growers a longer picking window for fresh eating, jams, and pies.
